questions.question: Define pure culture. / a). Culture containing many b). Culture contaminated with fungi species c). Population of cells arising from d). Mixed microbial population a single cell
questions.solution_html:
• Answer: c) Population of cells arising from a single cell
  • The pure culture should produce the same disease when inoculated into a healthy host.
  • Stationary Phase
  •  Nutrients become limited.
  •  Waste products accumulate.
  •  Rate of cell growth equals rate of cell death.
  • Spread evenly using a sterile L-shaped glass spreader.
  • Meiosis
  • Reduction division producing haploid spores.
  • Methods of Sexual Reproduction
  • A. Planogametic Copulation
  • Fusion of motile gametes.
  • Example: Lower fungi
  • B. Gametangial Contact
  • Male and female gametangia come into contact and nuclei migrate through a fertilization tube.
  • Example:Pythium
  • C. Gametangial Copulation
  • Entire gametangia fuse and their contents unite.
  • Example:Rhizopus
  • D. Spermatization

  • Example: Rust fungi

  • Fusion of ordinary vegetative cells.
  • Example: Mushrooms

  •  Generates genetic variation.
  •  Helps adaptation.
  •  Produces resistant spores.
  • Glutaraldehyde
  •  High-level disinfectant.
  •  Used for endoscopes and surgical instruments.

questions.question: State the contributions of Robert Koch and outline Koch’s postulates.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • Contributions of Robert Koch
  • Robert Koch is known as the Father of Medical Microbiology. His major contributions include
  •  Established the germ theory of disease.
  •  Identified Bacillus anthracis as the cause of anthrax.
  •  Discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis.
  •  Identified Vibrio cholerae as the causative organism of cholera.
  •  Developed pure culture techniques.
  •  Introduced staining methods and solid culture media.
  • Koch’s Postulates

questions.question: Define putrefaction and explain its significance in meat spoilage.
questions.solution_html:
• Putrefaction is the microbial decomposition of proteins present in meat, resulting in the
  • formation of foul-smelling compounds.
  • Significance in Meat Spoilage
  •  Produces ammonia, hydrogen sulfide, indole and skatole.
  •  Causes offensive odours.
  •  Alters flavour and texture.
  •  Reduces nutritional quality.
  •  Makes meat unsuitable for consumption.

questions.question: Describe the role of moisture in spoilage of stored cereal grains.
questions.solution_html:
• Moisture plays a major role in grain spoilage.
  • Effects of High Moisture
  •  Promotes growth of moulds and bacteria.
  •  Increases respiration of grains.
  •  Causes heating and caking.
  •  Encourages insect infestation.
  •  Leads to production of mycotoxins such as aflatoxins.
  •  Reduces shelf life and quality.
  • Prevention
  •  Maintain grain moisture below 13–14%.
  •  Store in dry and well-ventilated conditions.
  • Essay

questions.question: Explain Vibrio cholerae and Cholera in detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium responsible for cholera, a severe diarrheal disease.
  • Characteristics
  •  Gram-negative curved rod.
  •  Motile with polar flagellum.
  •  Non-spore-forming.
  •  Facultative anaerobe.
  • Sources
  •  Contaminated water.
  •  Contaminated food.
  •  Poor sanitation systems.
  • Transmission
  • Occurs through the fecal-oral route by consuming contaminated food and water.
  • Pathogenesis

questions.question: Describe the spoilage of milk with reference to acid, proteolytic, and gas-forming spoilage.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • Introduction
  • Milk is a highly nutritious food and serves as an excellent medium for microbial growth, leading to
  • spoilage.
  • A. Acid Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Lactobacillus
  •  Lactococcus
  •  Streptococcus
  • Process
  • Lactose is converted into lactic acid.
  • Effects
  •  Sour taste.
  •  Increased acidity.
  •  Coagulation of casein.
  •  Curd formation.
  • B. Proteolytic Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Pseudomonas
  •  Bacillus
  •  Clostridium
  • Process
  • Proteins are broken down by microbial enzymes.
  • Effects
  •  Bitter taste.
  •  Putrid odour.
  •  Texture deterioration.
  • C. Gas-forming Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Coliform bacteria
  •  Clostridium species
  •  Certain yeasts
  • Process
  • Fermentation of lactose produces carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
  • Effects
  •  Swollen containers.
  •  Foaming.
  •  Unpleasant taste and odour.
  • Prevention of Milk Spoilage
  •  Proper pasteurization.
  •  Refrigerated storage.
  •  Hygienic handling and packaging.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

  • A. Acid Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Lactobacillus
  •  Lactococcus
  •  Streptococcus
  • Process
  • Lactose is converted into lactic acid.
  • Effects
  •  Sour taste.
  •  Increased acidity.
  •  Coagulation of casein.
  •  Curd formation.
  • B. Proteolytic Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Pseudomonas
  •  Bacillus
  •  Clostridium
  • Process
  • Proteins are broken down by microbial enzymes.
  • Effects
  •  Bitter taste.
  •  Putrid odour.
  •  Texture deterioration.
  • C. Gas-forming Spoilage
  • Causative Organisms
  •  Coliform bacteria
  •  Clostridium species
  •  Certain yeasts
  • Process
  • Fermentation of lactose produces carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
  • Effects
  •  Swollen containers.
  •  Foaming.
  •  Unpleasant taste and odour.
  • Prevention of Milk Spoilage
  •  Proper pasteurization.
  •  Refrigerated storage.
  •  Hygienic handling and packaging.
